Declare the nesting hierarchy for a cohort

Source: R/hierarchy.R
cf_hierarchy.Rd

A cf_hierarchy describes how observational units are nested within each other (e.g., participants within clusters within sites). It is an ordered named list mapping role names to column name(s) in the data.

Usage

cf_hierarchy(...)

Arguments

...

Named arguments mapping role labels to column names, e.g. participant = "participant_id", cluster = "cluster_id". A role's value may be a character vector of more than one column when the level is a composite (multi-column) key, e.g. cluster_period = c("cluster_id", "period") for a stepped-wedge design. At least one entry is required.

Value

A cf_hierarchy object (a named list with additional class attribute).

Details

The order of ... is from the finest (innermost) level to the coarsest (outermost) level. The first role is conventionally the individual participant.

See also

Other pipeline: apply_criteria(), cf_expected(), continue_criteria()

Examples

# Two-level: participants within clusters
cf_hierarchy(participant = "pid", cluster = "cid")
#> Cohort hierarchy (finest → coarsest):
#>   ├─ participant  →  column: pid
#>   └─ cluster  →  column: cid

# Three-level: participants within clusters within sites
cf_hierarchy(participant = "pid", cluster = "cluster_id", site = "site_id")
#> Cohort hierarchy (finest → coarsest):
#>   ├─ participant  →  column: pid
#>   ├─ cluster  →  column: cluster_id
#>   └─ site  →  column: site_id

# Composite (multi-column) level: stepped-wedge cluster-period
cf_hierarchy(participant = "pid",
             cluster_period = c("cluster_id", "period"),
             cluster = "cluster_id")
#> Cohort hierarchy (finest → coarsest):
#>   ├─ participant  →  column: pid
#>   ├─ cluster_period  →  column: cluster_id + period
#>   └─ cluster  →  column: cluster_id
